title: Manatees and Sand Tiger Sharks Use Gas to Stay Afloat
summary:
Flatulence, the release of gas from the body’s lower opening, might seem like an unlikely survival tool. Yet some aquatic animals use the gas inside their bodies to help control their position in the water.

Florida manatees provide one example. According to data scientist and animal-flatulence author Nick Caruso, they can store gas in their guts. The gas may come from swallowed air or from digestion. Because gas is less dense than water, it increases buoyancy: the tendency to float rather than sink.

Manatees mainly eat seagrass in Florida’s shallow waters. These plants are difficult to digest, so the animals rely on a large hindgut, the rear part of the digestive tract. Microbes living there help break down the food, producing gas in the process.

The animals also have strong abdominal muscles and a powerful diaphragm, the muscle involved in breathing. These muscles can compress gas in the intestines and force some out. Releasing gas can help a manatee dive deeper. What people might dismiss as an awkward bodily function can therefore play a practical role underwater.

Sand tiger sharks use air for buoyancy too, but their method differs. Many bony fish have a swim bladder, an organ containing gas that helps them float. Sharks and rays lack both bones and swim bladders. Sharks’ oily livers help support them because oil is lighter than water, although many sharks still keep swimming to avoid sinking.

Marine conservation biologist David Shiffman explains that sand tiger sharks can sometimes hover instead. They gulp air at the surface and use it to help them stay in the water column. Shiffman says these sharks have been observed expelling air through their cloaca.

A cloaca is an opening used for waste and reproduction. Birds, reptiles, amphibians, sharks and some fish have one. Most mammals, by contrast, have separate routes for urine and feces. These anatomical differences mean that gas does not leave every animal in exactly the same way.

Some turtles have another unusual use for a cloaca that is separate from flatulence. Zoologist Dani Rabaiotti explains that they pump water into it, allowing oxygen from the water to enter their blood. Australia’s white-throated snapping turtle obtains 48 percent of its oxygen this way when in water.

These examples show why studying animal bodies can turn a funny question into useful biology. Gas storage, gas release and oxygen uptake are different processes, but each can help explain how particular animals function underwater.
why_it_matters: The article connects buoyancy, digestion and oxygen uptake to concrete animal examples, showing how different body processes help animals function underwater.
